newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH GOVERNMENT NARROWLY SURVIVES CONFIDENCE VOTE.
newsitem.headline: CZECH GOVERNMENT NARROWLY SURVIVES CONFIDENCE VOTE.

text.p: The centre-right Czech coalition government on Wednesday narrowly won a vote of confidence in the lower house of parliament after giving into demands that the chamber get a say in key bank and utility privatisations.

In a dramatic vote along party lines, Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus and his cabinet squeezed out the minimum necessary support in the 200-seat house, as a single independent deputy joined the three-party ruling coalition's 100 votes.
"The government is ready to take on this work, knowing that it will not be applauded for everything it does now," Klaus told the chamber after winning the vote.
Klaus called for the confidence measure on Tuesday as the cabinet submitted its programme aimed at answering an economic downturn and a sharp depreciation in the Czech crown.

The vote, which analysts expected Klaus to win earlier in the day after Communist deputy Miroslav Vacek announced he would not attend because of a serious illness, was thrown into doubt when Vacek showed up just before voting began.
This made the vote of an independent deputy, budget committee chairman Jozef Wagner, crucial to the government.
Wagner made his support conditional on the house getting a say on privatisations of major banks and utilities which have already been proposed by the finance ministry.

Klaus, who rejected Wagner's suggestion just minutes before the vote, reversed himself following a hastily called meeting with Wagner soon after Vacek arrived, and said the cabinet would submit the privatisations to the house.

The government called the vote as it submitted an austerity programme cutting an additional 20 billion crowns in spending and social transfers from the 1997 budget aiming to cut domestic demand and stem a huge current account deficit.

Klaus, an economist credited as the main architect of the post-communist Czech economic transformation and who has been sharply criticised as the economy has soured, would have been forced to step down if the government lost the vote.

The austerity package followed two turbulent weeks in the foreign exchange market when investors, alarmed at a widening current account gap and mounting political uncertainty, dumped the crown forcing the central bank to float the currency.
"We should not forget that the Czech Republic was up to now considered an economically and politically stable country and that was a success for us all," Klaus told the house before the vote.
"We should agree that it is in our national interest to preserve this credit, and never irreparably damage it or lose it," he said.
Wagner was expelled from the opposition Social Democrats after he voted with the government and gave Klaus a narrow victory in approving the 1997 budget late last year.

He said after the Tuesday vote he was happy his manouvre effectively delayed the privatisation of Komercni Banka a.s. and Ceskovslovenska Obchodni Banka a.s. which was scheduled for discussion in Thursday's government agenda.

"Clear divides between industrial companies and banks have to be sorted out and then the 'cleaned' companies could be privatised... otherwise I will not support the privatisation," Wagner told reporters after the vote.
Milos Zeman, leader of the main opposition Social Democrats, told the house before the vote that Klaus's government did not deserve trust.
"I want to express my deep conviction that the basic factor of economic instability in the Czech Republic is the current government in its current personnel composition," Zeman said.
